planting.note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in moist, well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light; unlike the plain-green species, Bianca needs a bit more light to hold its white variegation and can revert to solid green in deep shade.

directions: Bianca is a variegated sport of turtle vine, its tiny rounded leaves streaked and edged in creamy white against the plain green background of the species, giving trailing stems a frosted, two-tone look. The white portions carry less chlorophyll than solid-green leaves, so Bianca grows a touch slower and holds its pattern best with a few hours of bright, indirect light rather than the deeper shade the straight species tolerates. Like other Callisia repens forms it roots from almost any stem node, making it simple to propagate fresh cuttings whenever a hanging basket or terrarium planting starts looking sparse or reverts to green. Keep the mix lightly moist and well drained, since the succulent leaves and stems are prone to rot if left soggy.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Foliage Plants

planting.note: Pot up nursery-trained specimens any time indoors in fast-draining bonsai or houseplant mix in bright indirect light; grown strictly as a container/bonsai subject, it lacks the incidental cold tolerance mature landscape Ficus microcarpa develop outdoors.

directions: Ginseng fig is a specialty bonsai form of Indian laurel selected and trained for its thick, bulbous, exposed root mass rather than the towering canopy of the straight species, giving container specimens a gnarled, aged look within just a few years. Small, glossy, oval leaves emerge densely along a compact branching structure that responds well to pruning and wiring, making it one of the most widely sold beginner bonsai subjects in nurseries and home centers. Grow it indoors year-round in bright indirect light, since it drops leaves readily when moved or chilled and has none of the frost tolerance mature landscape-grown Ficus microcarpa can develop. Let the top inch of fast-draining bonsai mix dry between waterings, mist occasionally to counter dry indoor air, and repot every one to two years to refresh the soil around the swollen root crown.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ficus microcarpa

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in bright light with some direct morning sun; grow primarily as a houseplant or patio plant, since the variegated leaf margins are more cold-sensitive than the plain green species.

directions: Variegata carries an irregular creamy white margin around each tiny oval leaf, brightening the fine-textured, densely branched habit that makes Serissa such a popular bonsai and container subject. Like the green species it produces a long, nearly continuous flush of small white star-shaped flowers, but the pale leaf edges need consistently bright light to stay crisp; plants kept too dim tend to lose their white margin and revert toward plain green. Its variegated leaves carry less chlorophyll than the species, so growth is a little slower and the plant benefits from steady warmth and even moisture rather than the wider swings the straight species can shrug off. As with other Serissa, avoid moving it around or letting it dry out, since sudden changes in light or watering trigger leaf drop.
